items.title: Differences between both Apple HomeView models revealed in teardown
items.content_html:
A new teardown of both the speaker base and wall-mounted options for Apple HomeView reveals several details, like smaller speakers in the wall-mounted options and poor repairability.

Apple HomeView was announced on October 13 as the company's first-ever smart home hub. With it, you can use Siri to control smart locks and cameras, get information from the web, and interact with some apps like those enabled for CarPlay.

It wasn't clear whether Apple simply built a tablet device and sold one with a speaker base attached when Apple HomeView was revealed. Thanks to a teardown from iFixit, we now know that isn't the case.

The wall-mounted option has smaller speakers and small tweaks to the internal layout. The model with an included speaker base has larger speakers behind the display.

Apple clearly wants the music experience to be as good as possible on the Apple HomeView with speaker base. Though, given these differences, it seems odd that Apple charges the same price for both since you're getting a worse experience and less gear with the wall-mounted option.

Still, as noted in the Apple HomeView teardown, the two models have one thing in common: poor repairability in nearly every area. It all has to do with the seemingly excessive amounts of glue Apple used for assembly.

On both models, the display is held in place with strong adhesive, making it difficult to remove even with suction cups. Glue is also used to secure the speakers and speaker connectors, both of which broke during an attempted removal as part of the teardown.

As if that wasn't enough, Apple also managed to use a different type of glue to secure thermal shielding underneath the main logic board. All of this makes replacing the speakers, speaker connectors, and display difficult.

On the logic board of the Apple HomeView, all the important chips are soldered to the board. This includes the A18 system-on-chip, an 8GB RAM chip from SK Hynix, and a 64GB NAND chip made by Kioxia.

As for the speaker base version, repairability is only slightly better. Though the USB-C port is replaceable, removing the woofer inside the base is made difficult by a short speaker cable and screws that sit at an odd angle.

iFixit notes that the Apple HomeView is not as repairable as Apple's latest devices. This could be related to Apple HomeView reportedly being ready to go for more than a year, but was held back due to delays in Siri AI feature launches.

Given the HomeView is an entirely new product category, there's plenty of room for improvement with subsequent generations. A new model with a larger 9-inch display and articulating arm is expected in 2027.

items.title: 'Not a cyber attack,' Apple says about outage that hit iCloud & internal services
items.content_html:
Some of Apple's online services had problems Tuesday, with iCloud Accounts, iCloud Mail, Apple Business, AppleCare on Device, and some school services down.

While Apple and other companies strive for 100% uptime, that's never going to be the case for something of its size and catalog of servers. On Tuesday, it endured a number of outages that affected its users.

The Apple System Status page listed eight issues, with three filed as outages, and one resolved.

The initial non-outage was for iCloud Account & Sign In, which was listed as being slow or unavailable and affected all users. It started at 11:45 a.m. Eastern and was resolved in the afternoon.

The four original outages started with AppleCare on Device, which affected all users as of 11:15 a.m. ET, but was resolved at 3:39 p.m. AppleCare purchasing was temporarily unavailable but was also resolved at 3:39 p.m.

Apple Business was also listed as slow or unavailable, affecting some users. That started at 1:40 p.m. Eastern, and was later downgraded to an issue.

Apple School Manager and Schoolwork rounded out the outages, before downgrading to issues. Both started at 1:40 p.m. Eastern, affect "some" users, and were slow or unavailable.

Schoolwork was resolved at 3:00 p.m. ET.

At 2:03 p.m. ET, Apple updated the list to include outages for iCloud Mail and iCloud Web Apps, namely iCloud.com. Both were again affecting "some" users" who were unable to use the service, but iCloud issues were resolved at 1:25 p.m.

A later update introduced an outage for the App Store at 2:27 p.m. as well as a Volume Purchasing Program outage at the same time. Both were updated to "resolved" at 3 p.m.

Public and developer

The problems weren't just on the consumer side of things. There were also issues for developers too.

The Developer System Status page listed a total of nine incidents for Tuesday. All were resolved by 7:10 p.m. ET except for two App Store Connect outages that are still ongoing.

Four of the day's outages were for App Store Connect, with two specifically covering Analytics as well as Sales and Trends. The Analytics and Sales and Trends outages were resolved at 7 p.m. ET.

There was a similar issue mentioned for Xcode Cloud, which affected all users until about 4 p.m. ET.

Apple Music Connect and Apple Music for Artists had problems that emerged at the same time, 2:09 p.m. ET. Both were resolved at 7 p.m.

The sole issue on the list was News Publisher, with it apparently having performance problems until about 4:20 p.m. ET.

The first resolved outage was for the App Store, concerning in-app purchases. That was a problem that ran from 5:28 a.m. Eastern until 6:46 a.m. ET.

Internal as well as external

This time, the outages weren't just externally-facing services. It seems to have also affected internal tools and services.

According to Bloomberg, the outages were caused by an internal update. This included employee portal AppleWeb, internal sign-in system AppleConnect, and VPN access for remote workers, an anonymous source claimed.

Employees couldn't download internal software builds, book conference rooms, nor access company calendars. Systems requiring Apple credentials also went down, leaving employees unable to work.

Apple Stores around the world were also apparently affected by the issues.

"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," Apple shared in a statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible."

Apple also emphasized that the problems didn't originate from a cyber attack. The outages affecting most customers and users have been resolved.

Updated on 17 November, 2026 at 2:39 p.m. ET: Changed listed issues and added context.

Updated on 17 November, 2026 at 3:29 p.m. ET: Changed statuses.

Updated on 17 November, 2026 at 3:59 p.m. ET: Changed statuses.

Updated on 17 November, 2026 at 5:00 p.m. ET: Consumer-facing outages resolved, some developer outages still ongoing.

Updated on 17 November, 2026 at 10:25 p.m. ET: All issues and outages resolved minus two with App Store Connect.

items.title: Google Wallet arrives on iPhone, but you'll still need Apple Pay at the register
items.content_html:
Google Wallet is coming to iPhone to organize tickets, track deliveries, and manage agentic purchases; unfortunately, its usefulness stops short of the checkout counter.

Google Wallet is giving iPhone users another option for digital wallet management. Users can manage payment cards to check out online across Google and anywhere that accepts Google Pay.

It also syncs with Gmail and Google apps, allowing users to organize package tracking, digital boarding passes, concert tickets, and receipts. Users can also scan loyalty and membership cards with the camera to import them into Google Wallet.

According to the press release, Google Wallet will also be a secure hub for managing agentic purchases across Google. It says users can easily view and manage order confirmations, receipts, and delivery updates in one secure place.

You can download Google Wallet from the App Store. It requires iOS 17.0 or later.

There is no tap-to-pay support for Google Wallet on iOS. Users will still need Apple Pay for that functionality.

items.title: Apple is accused of ordering iPhone Duo supplier to stop denying hinge faults
items.content_html:
Apple has been accused of forcing a component supplier to take down statements distancing it from the iPhone Duo's hinge problems.

While the number of iPhone Duo screens cracking appears to have been very small, it was large enough for Apple to acknowledge it. Shortly before Apple made that announcement, though, component manufacturer Fine M-Tec made one of its own.

Depending on the translation used, Fine M-Tec either referred to just "some foldable smartphones," or didn't even go that far. But what the company definitely did do was state that there were no defects in the parts it provided to a customer.

Fine M-Tec did not name Apple, and it has supplied hinge components to Samsung. But its denial was issued as iPhone Duo complaints mounted, so it was presumed that the customer referred to was Apple.

Now it's claimed that this Fine M-Tec statement has been withdrawn. That can't be confirmed because of how the original source for the report of Fine M-Tec's statement, The Elec, showed a screengrab instead of including a verifiable link.

Nonetheless, it's now been claimed that The Elec ran a follow-up editorial saying that Fine M-Tec had removed its statements. It's also been claimed that a representative of the supplier then asked the publication to withdraw that subsequent article.

That representative is reported to have said that Apple had objected to Fine M-Tec speaking publicly about the matter. These most recent developments were first spotted by MacRumors.

Confusing accounts

However, at time of writing there appears to be no sign of The Elec's reported editorial, nor a piece about Apple pressing the supplier over the issue. The original report of Fine M-Tec's statement is still available online.

Unsurprisingly, neither Apple nor Fine M-Tec has since commented publicly.

What has separately emerged is that the hinge component concerned is believed to be sourced from two suppliers. It's not known which firm other than Fine M-Tec provides this component.

But then it wouldn't be known that Fine M-Tec was a supplier if the company itself hadn't denied blame. And threatened legal action against anyone accusing it of producing faulty components.

The hinge problems with the iPhone Duo, though, now do appear to be specifically because of a material failure in the hinge, rather than a symptom of a poor design.

items.title: Apple board member and former chair about to sell $32 million in AAPL
items.content_html: Arthur Levinson is selling a large amount of his AAPL holdings. In a new SEC filing, Levinson has disclosed that he is selling 90,000 shares originally valued at $31,500 in 2000. There's no stated reason for the sale, but the fact that he's 76 years old might have something to do with it.

items.title: Jensen Huang says he'll return to Nvidia if he gets asked
items.content_html:
Disgraced ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has finally spoken about his resignation and desire to return to the company following the exposure of his affair with a Chinese spy and two other staffers.

Nvidia's board continued to back Huang after news emerged of his first affair with a suspected Chinese spy. But that changed after a second affair was revealed, and after the firm's market valuation dropped by over $800 billion.

Jensen Huang resigned following a board meeting on November 12. It's unclear if Huang was asked to resign or be fired, or if he made the decision on his own.

And now, after public statements by Donald Trump and Elon Musk supporting Huang, he says that he'll return if he's asked.

"Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said in a short statement first reported by the Wall Street Journal. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia," Huang added. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely."

Assuming the board does not ask for his return, and they do not appear to be considering it, it's likely to take some time for Nvidia to appoint a permanent new CEO. Nvidia is said to be looking at offering the position to Johny Srouji.

If this is true, and if Srouji takes the job, Apple would lose one of the key figures behind its Apple Silicon development.

Nvidia's stock has fallen from a high of about $221 on October 21 to $155 or so at publication time. The stock has been down all day but has risen a bit in the last half hour, likely on this news.

items.title: This is what the iPhone 20 Pro curved glass screen could look like
items.content_html:
A video claims to show the curved glass panel that will appear at the front of the iPhone 20 Pro, hinting at the anniversary iPhone's design.

The front screen of the iPhone is a dominant feature, with the glass covering it an important part of the overall design. While there have been many rumors about the iPhone 20 Pro having a curved display, there's no way for people to truly visualize what that could look like.

A video released to X by serial leaker Ice Universe shows a curved glass panel on a stand. Accompanying it is a comment about the iPhone 20 Pro having a "milestone design," with the leaker insinuating that the glass in the video is from that device.

The glass itself isn't massively remarkable, with it having two holes at the top for the front camera system. Around the edge is a thin black bezel, which again isn't really a change from the norm.

The Apple iPhone 20 Pro is going to feature a milestone design - let's take a look first

— Ice Universe (@UniverseIce) November 16, 2026

The main talking point for the glass is the amount of curvature on the edges and corners, leading the top surface to stick out. While there has been some curves at the edges of recent iPhone displays, this seems to be a little more pronounced.

To be clear, there is no guarantee that the panel being displayed is an actual component for the iPhone 20 Pro. With its release just under a year away, it could be a test component at best.

It is more likely to be an attempt by an accessory manufacturer to come up with a screen protector for the design, long in advance of Apple's announcement.

As a leaker, Ice Universe has a reasonably good track record, but it's still best to take any rumor with a pinch of salt.

A curved marvel

So far, rumors about the iPhone 20 Pro's design have followed the same sort of lines. Especially when looking at claims made over the summer.

Weibo-based leaker Fixed Focus Digital said on August 3 that the glass-heavy base-model iPhone 20 design will borrow design elements from the iPhone Air. Chiefly made from glass, it will be a relatively thin design with an iPhone Air-like mid-frame construction.

Another leaker insisted a week later that the model will have a bezel-less effect because of the glass cover. The aim of the curved glass is to use optical refraction to create a borderless effect, they said.

Later in the month, a leaker added that it would use the same glass assembly as the iPhone Air, but with more rounded components. But this time with claims of heat dissipation improvements.

More recently, on November 16, leaker Fixed Focus Digital reiterated the more-rounded iPhone Air claim, but said it also applied to the iPhone 20 Pro. They also backed up another rumor from May 2026 that Apple was using a quad-curved OLED display for the Pro model.

There are plenty of rumors about the glass being curved. As such, take the video as inspiration of how the glass may appear on the iPhone 20 Pro, rather than absolute fact.

items.title: Trump administration backs down after pushing Apple to pull ICE tracking app
items.content_html:
The government settled a lawsuit after a judge found its demands to pull Eyes Up from the App Store likely violated its creator's First Amendment rights.

The settlement makes the injunction permanent and requires federal officials to notify Apple and Meta of the court order. The case also covered a Chicago Facebook page that Meta took down after federal officials pressed for its removal.

"I'm glad the government agreed to stop targeting my speech, but it shouldn't take a lawsuit to get the government to respect our constitutional rights," Eyes Up creator Mark Hodges said in a statement seen by Indie Star. "People have a right to know what their government is doing."

"I hope that thanks to this lawsuit, others can share what they see and hear without facing this kind of censorship."

Mark Hodges created Eyes Up to collect user-submitted videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity. Apple removed the app from the App Store after repeated takedown demands from the federal government.

In February 2026, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) announced that it would sue Attorney General Pam Bondi and Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem. The suit centered on First Amendment obstruction, and represented both Eyes Up and a Chicago-based Facebook group used for reporting ICE incidents.

As a result, a judge found that the government likely violated their First Amendment rights by pressuring Apple and Meta to remove ICE-tracking apps and Facebook pages. The resulting order required the government to stop that pressure and notify both companies of the ruling.

More suits and rulings are pending. The ICEblock developer is suing as well.

items.title: Apple Pencil on iPhone Duo is the bare-minimum experience, but works
items.content_html:
You can't pair Apple Pencil with USB-C to an iPhone Duo without a cable, it has nowhere to go when it isn't being used, and lacks many features. Still, it's enough for casual stylus use.

I am not an artist, handwritten note-taker, or avid Apple Pencil user. The most I do these days is keep track of tasks in paper notebooks for easy reference.

Yet, I've always been drawn to owning whatever Apple Pencil I needed to use with the devices in my collection. Apple is on its fourth Apple Pencil in its lineup, and it was yet another I had to purchase since iPhone Duo has such specific requirements.

If you're interested in using Apple Pencil on iPhone Duo, the only option is Apple Pencil with USB-C. Third-party options like Logitech Crayon won't work, though there are already some unofficial stylus that claim to work with iPhone Duo on Amazon.

None of Apple's other options work either. The USB-C port is the only available pairing method.

Overall, the experience is what you'd expect. Here's how Apple Pencil with USB-C works on iPhone Duo.

The good: Drawing on two displays

The outer display feels like the perfect little notepad when writing with Apple Pencil. If you like the act of jotting down handwritten notes, there's nothing better for it.

You can draw on iPhone Duo, but not flat on a table

There is no give in the glossy outer display so it feels like writing with Apple Pencil on any iPad. Though, since the Apple Pencil with USB-C lacks haptics and other features, it feels a little dead.

While I'm sure there are plenty of artists out there that will doodle on the outer display, it's the inner display that is the true canvas. Open up the iPhone Duo and you're met with plenty of writing or drawing space.

The inner display has some give thanks to being a flexible plastic material. I still feel a little worry when sketching on the inner display since I'm not sure how well it will hold up over time.

From my minimal writing and doodles, there aren't any visible issues so far. It will be interesting to hear from those that use the Apple Pencil more regularly over time.

Highlight text in Apple Books

iOS is built so it can be mostly navigated with Apple Pencil, plus you can use features like Scribble to write letters in text fields. I'm still not sure why you'd ever use Scribble, but it's there.

Apps like Apple Books has the option to highlight text with Apple Pencil. You can also draw in apps like Freeform, Notes, and Apple Journal.

I'm glad Apple Pencil support is finally on an iPhone, but it only really makes sense because of the wide outer display and large inner display.

The bad: If you see a stylus, they blew it

Apple Pencil support on iPhone Duo shouldn't be any surprise if you've ever used it on iPad. That said, the Apple Pencil with USB-C makes the whole thing less enjoyable.

Simple writing, drawing, and annotating are possible on iPhone Duo

I may have cited Steve Jobs' famous quote here, but only because he was referring to stylus use on smartphones. Even then, he was pointing to devices that necessitated a stylus over touch.

Anyway, Apple Pencil is a great product, but the USB-C model is far from the ideal experience. I've been spoiled by every other model, yes, that includes the weird first-generation.

Here's the thing — there is no guarantee that when you pick up the Apple Pencil with USB-C that it'll just work.

On a few occasions, I've gone to use the Apple Pencil with USB-C only to find it wouldn't wake up. There are no buttons to press, and tapping it on the iPhone Duo does nothing.

No, the only way to get the device to wake at that point is plugging it into power or into the iPhone. That means I'll need to make sure I at least have a cable on me when carrying the Apple Pencil.

Nowhere to put Apple Pencil when not in use

This experience alone makes it almost not worth it. Almost.

Another annoyance is the iPhone Duo makes for a bad canvas. You'll absolutely have to hold it with one hand, open or closed, to draw or write on it thanks to the camera bump.

I'm sure some cases or stands will be better for artists, but it isn't an option to lay it flat on a table out of the box. It's just not a good drawing tablet in the traditional sense.

I don't know how much I'll use Apple Pencil with iPhone Duo, but I'm glad it is an option.

Apple Pencil mini would be great

The lack of a mounting point for Apple Pencil is perhaps my biggest gripe with the iPhone Duo experience. At least on iPad it can awkwardly magnetically attach to an edge.

It's time for an Apple Pencil rethink

The lack of mounting means no means of charging or pairing with iPhone Duo, at least not without a cable. I'm sure some case manufacturers will make bespoke Apple Pencil holders, but it won't help much.

The Apple Pencil with USB-C is just too long.

What I'd like to see is something in the middle of Apple's first-generation model and the Logitech Crayon. Give me an iPhone Duo stylus with magnetic mounting that's as short as the Duo's hinge side while being easy to hold.

I'd even take a weird USB-C tip in the end if only so I can connect it to my iPhone Duo without needing a cable.

The Apple Pencil with USB-C lacks pressure sensitivity, double tap, barrel roll, squeeze, haptics, and Find My. Hover isn't an option on iPhone Duo either.

Perhaps it is too late for this first generation of iPhone Duo, but it would be nice to see a second-generation model launch with a bespoke stylus. I used a Samsung Galaxy with a built-in stylus that was interesting, though it was a passive stylus versus the computationally interactive Apple Pencil.

I believe Apple can come up with a smart solution in future generations. In the meantime, I guess we'll just need to see what clever accessory makers can come up with.

items.title: You can use Apple's self-repair program for iPhone Duo now
items.content_html: Apple's Self Repair Program has expanded again, now adding parts and repair procedures for the iPhone Duo. As always, we recommend that users have at least some experience with repair before they try to repair an iPhone, as it is extremely easy to make the problem worse, not better.

items.title: iPhone, iPad targeted by massive website malware attack
items.content_html:
Visitors to over 170 major websites may have been affected by malicious code inserted through Optimizely trying to steal crypto and credit card data, with one vector of the attack focused on iPhones and iPads.

While websites are frequently used as the attack vector to affect as many people as possible, it's rare for it to affect many major sites simultaneously. However, one part of the attack affecting the tool has potentially impacted iPhone users hanging on to older versions of iOS and iPadOS.

A flaw was found in Optimizely, a web experimentation platform for testing website elements, which enabled an attacker to place malicious JavaScript code. This code was then shown to users of websites that use the tool, potentially infecting viewers.

For iPhone and iPad, that script had a second stage that used iOS exploit kits, referred to as Coruna and DarkSword

However, it is claimed by Optimizely that no iPhones were actively taken over in an attack. There were still victims, as it is believed that about $7,000 in cryptocurrency was taken in about nine hours.

Hacker News reports that websites from at least 178 organizations were affected on November 16, with the list including:

  • Air France-KLM
  • BBC
  • CNN
  • Equifax
  • HSBC
  • Ikea
  • Ledger
  • Peacock
  • Salesforce
  • Zoom

What happened?

The attack was based on an attacker adding malicious code to many projects held in Optimizely accounts. However, a breakdown from Report URI says it is still unknown how the attacker managed to get write access to accounts that were not supposed to be under their control.

Optimizely Web usually works by websites loading a Javascript snippet from the company's CDN, which contains both Optimizely's code and a customer's experimental code. A third optional field called Project Javascript is in the snippet, which is custom code the customer writes that runs on every page.

The attacker used Project Javascript to insert their own code, leaving the rest of the snippet untouched. The snippet was then able to be served from the CDN using Optimizely's security certificate, which affected sites already trusted.

The scripts hosted code that would replace the crypto wallet addresses on affected devices, if successful. The replaced addresses lead to accounts controlled by the attacker.

There were multiple versions of injected code, with one including a card skimmer. The code would capture the card number, expiry date, and CVV number of cards submitted through the site's form fields, transmitting them to the attacker's server.

Optimizely says that the vulnerability in its service has been fixed, with injected code removed from affected projects. It has also taken steps to secure affected accounts and to introduce more protections to prevent such an attack from happening again.

What you need to do

Anyone who visited an affected website on Monday should update their iPhones and iPads to iOS 26.3 or later. For older models, that means updating to iOS 18.7.3 or later.

It seems that, for those who kept their devices up to date, they probably wouldn't have been affected by the attack at all.

If they made a card payment on any affected website, they should also check their card statements for fraudulent transactions that may happen in the future.

Cryptocurrency owners should also check any payments made, including the addresses they intended to pay, in case they were swapped.

items.title: PSA: Your iPhone won't sound during Tuesday's Emergency Alert System alarm test
items.content_html:
Don't be startled if you hear an emergency alert on your tv or radio, but not your iPhone. FEMA and the FCC are performing a test of the legacy U.S. Emergency Alert System.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) will be issuing an Emergency Alert System test at approximately 2:20 pm Eastern on November 17. This is to test that a message sent to broadcasters goes through correctly, in preparation for future emergencies.

Like previous tests, this will take the form of a loud high-pitched alarm noise, with a message on your TV or radio announcer explaining it is just a test.

FEMA is required to test the National Wireless Emergency Alert System at least once every three years. The last one of its kind took place on October 4, 2023.

The public notice of the test from the FCC, dated September 16, says the message will warn that it is a nationwide test covering the United States, and that no action is required from the public.

Update 8:00 AM ET, November 17, 2026: We were operating from an outdated statement from FEMA about the test. The test will be on conventional broadcast systems like radio, television, and satelite communications,and not your iPhone. AppleInsider regrets the error.

items.title: Chip shortage forces Apple to sign long-term contract with Samsung
items.content_html:
Apple is reportedly close to securing supplies of DRAM for the iPhone for the next several years, but on terms that appear unusually favorable for supplier Samsung.

Apple had managed to ride out the global chip shortage for some time because of existing orders. However, by February 2026, it was reportedly having to agree to pay double its previous amount for DRAM.

That deal was with Samsung and appears to have been for some or all of 2026. Now according to Korean news site Maeil Business Newspaper, Samsung is at least close to securing a deal that should see it supplying DRAM to Apple until 2031 or 2032.

It's specifically a four- or five-year long-term agreement (LTA) contract. There will be a minimum order quantity in the LTA, but the pricing will alter depending on market conditions.

"Considering Apple's existing characteristics," an unspecified semiconductor official told the publication, "this LTA with Samsung is an unconventional contract that has been rare in the past."

Changing supplier landscape

It may have been rare for Apple, but it's claimed that all other Big Tech firms have already signed similar deals with Samsung. Then, too, Apple is reported to have entered into an LTA with memory supplier SK Hynix which may be similar.

The benefit to Samsung is that it secures orders and income for a protracted period. This would always have been the case, but now providing consumer DRAM for Apple is also a hedge against AI memory demand faltering.

In the short term, however, demand for RAM in the many AI data centers under construction around the world is what has driven prices up. It's not only RAM and DRAM that has been affected, either, as processor costs have also risen.

This is why Apple eventually raised the price of most of its devices in July 2026. It's also why there were price hikes on the refreshed models that launched in September and October.

It's very likely that there will be further price hikes in 2027.

items.title: Order an iPhone Duo now, and you'll probably get it before Christmas
items.content_html:
After iPhone Duo order dates slipped to the end of January 2027, Apple has brought them all forward, meaning they could now arrive before the holidays.

Online pre-orders for the iPhone Duo sold out instantly, and stocks were depleted almost as quickly at retail Apple Stores. There was some slight improvement after a couple of weeks, but now there is much more.

Ordering the iPhone Duo now in either color and with any of its storage capacities, gets a quoted shipping date of December 17-28, 2026. It's tight for Christmas Day, but it's hugely better than the previous estimate of January 26, 2027.

Buyers who had already ordered are also being told that their delivery dates have been brought forward significantly. One buyer told AppleInsider that they had originally been quoted January 2027, but instead received their iPhone Duo on November 16, 2026.

There's not enough information, even anecdotally, to determine how soon existing pre-orders are likely to ship. But with new orders just about beating the holidays, it should presumably be that existing orders arrive first.

As yet, the online Apple Store is showing no availability for order pickup at any physical store. It's previously been reported that Apple was concentrating on getting the iPhone Duo into stores for launch day, though, so it's likely that it aims to increase Apple Store stocks.

How Apple is doing this

Despite Apple saying that the demand for the iPhone Duo had been extraordinary, it has not and will not release figures. So it's not clear how many were even available at launch, and persistent rumors claimed supplies were limited because of production problems.

The date is still very close if you want to buy someone an iPhone Duo for the holidays, but it's a lot better than it has been.

There were then a pair of reports claiming that Apple was increasing production of the iPhone Duo. However, one was based on increased orders for components at certain manufacturers, and so ignored how Apple often switches suppliers.

The other specified that Apple had increased iPhone Duo orders by 30%. It made the same error conflating components with finished iPhones, but it was also based in part on some very dubious math.

Nonetheless, whether Apple has increased production or has just rectified manufacturing problems, it has now cut about a month off its previous delivery schedule.

items.title: 'Baby, this is Keke Palmer' is crowned Apple Podcasts' show of the year
items.content_html:
Apple has announced its Podcast of the Year is entertainer Keke Palmer's eponymous show, which brings listeners conversations with stars across show business and culture.

"Baby, this is Keke Palmer," has run for 200 episodes since 2023, and aims to consist of detailed conversations that go beyond promoting work, to instead discussing identity and relationships.

"Keke's curiosity, humor, and openness make every conversation feel personal, and video brings that connection even closer," Oliver Schusser, Apple's vice president of Podcasts, Music, Sports, and Beats, said in a statement. "Her exceptional craft and cultural impact make 'Baby, this is Keke Palmer' Apple Podcasts' Show of the Year."

"We're proud to celebrate her talent across Apple Podcasts and Apple Music, from the conversations she creates to the music she shares," he continued.

Palmer executive produces the show for Wondery, and says she's honored to have won this year's title.

"Thank you to Apple Podcasts, Wondery, our incredible guests, and everyone who listens and brings their own perspective to the conversation," she said. "This recognition means so much to me."

"I love how a conversation about entertainment can open up a bigger conversation about life," continued Palmer. "There's so much to explore in the things we watch, laugh at, and connect with, and this show gives me room to follow that curiosity."

Apple has been choosing a Podcast of the Year since 2020, when NPR's "Code Switch" won. Typically Apple will then support its choice with related content, this time with an Apple Music playlist for Keke Palmer.

This year's award follows the news that video podcasts are shortly to become available to watch on Apple TV 4K.

items.title: Keychron K2 Ultra 8K review: More affordable 8KHz polling & custom RGB
items.content_html:
Keychron makes a lot of keyboards, but the latest Ultra 8K line is the peak of their offering, while the K2 keeps those specs and premium design affordable.

I'll be honest, I had to comb through the specs page to understand exactly what was different about the Keychron K2 Ultra 8K versus the Q1 Ultra 8K I reviewed recently. That's a compliment considering this keyboard is half the price.

When shopping for Keychron keyboards, it is best to understand what each portion of the name represents. In this case, the K2 is a step down from the Q-series thanks to its metal frame versus full-metal body, plus some other small differences.

The Ultra 8K moniker refers to the 8,000 Hz polling rate, long battery life, and the powerful MCU chipset. It's a performant keyboard that can be customized top to bottom.

If you're looking for the best of Keychron, an Ultra 8K model is it, though you can get it at a much more reasonable price with the K2 series. Let's get into the details.

Keychron K2 Ultra 8K review: Design

Keychron has a signature design that becomes difficult to differentiate without being an expert on the product lines. The K2 Ultra 8K is a 75% layout keyboard with Apex red, brown, or banana switches.

I chose the Apex red switches and was also able to test the K8 Ultra 8K, though it is nearly identical besides the few extra keys. Between the two, I prefer the smaller layout that weighs less at 2.39 pounds.

The K lineup lacks a volume knob, which isn't ideal since that has proven to be a very useful option. Even so, the F keys still work for volume and such on iPad and Mac.

I've learned to love the south-facing RGB backlighting, which can be fully customized with Keychron Launcher. Colors can be assigned to glow on a per-key basis but there's also the several presets and animations built-in.

The keycaps themselves are quite boring. They're available in this dull gray color scheme with a green escape key, though they can be swapped with key caps of your choice.

I would love to see Keychron try out keycaps with passthrough letters.

The design is nothing flashy beyond the RGB backlighting. It's fairly standard for Keychron and will fit in anywhere.

The Apex red switches I tested have a nice clack but they're not loud. There's also more than enough foam to keep the reverb low.

The feedback is also pleasant as each key depresses with and returns easily. I never feel fatigue when typing with these switches and they remain my go-to.

As with any mechanical keyboard, there are many layers here:

  • Double-shot PBT keycaps
  • CNC-machined aluminum frame
  • Apex red, brown, or banana switches; hot swappable
  • Steel plate
  • EVA Foam
  • IXPE Foam and PET Film
  • PCB
  • EPDM Foam
  • Bottom case PET Film
  • Silicone bottom pad
  • ABS bottom case

The reduced price and weight comes down to build materials compared to other keyboards. Keychron's Q1 line, for example, has a full metal body.

Keychron K2 Ultra 8K review: Features

One of the most interesting aspects of covering Keychron over the years is the incredible battery life gains. The K2 Ultra 8K has up to 760 hours of backlight-off use.

My current desktop setup minimizes wires so my keyboard is wireless. I'll eventually get a dock and some wires in here, but that day isn't today.

The Keychron K2 Ultra 8K lasts through days of work before needing a charge. Having the K2 and K8 to test has been handy, as I just swap them out as needed (this is silly, don't do this).

Some of these advanced specs are a bit lost on me, but they're great if you need them. The 8,000 Hz polling rate means you'll never run into timing issues when gaming.

Connect to your Mac, iPad, or PC through a 2.4GHz dongle, Bluetooth 5.2, or wired connection. By using the switch on the side and three Bluetooth radios, you can easily swap between five devices without un-pairing or re-pairing a device.

My setup is complex, as I can easily be using or testing several products at once. The Keychron K2 Ultra 8K lets me easily swap between the 2.4GHz connection to my Mac and the Bluetooth connections to my Apple Vision Pro and iPad.

All of these features are powered by the Keychron MCU with 1MB flash. Connect to a Mac or PC and visit the Keychron Launcher to customize every keypress and even each RGB LED.

Do be sure to visit the customization software and toggle on the 8KHz setting. All Keychron 8K keyboards ship with 1KHz on by default to ensure the widest compatibility.

If I had a complaint about how the Keychron system works, it's that I can't do any customization on the iPad. I'd love to see Keychron Launcher work via an iPad app since I'm sure it'll never work in Safari.

Using the Keychron K2 Ultra 8K

I've enjoyed using the Keychron K2 Ultra 8K these past several weeks, though I'm ready to get back to premium metals and knobs. The K2 series was the first mechanical keyboard I ever reviewed, and I still find it a perfect entry point into the hobby.

Keychron keyboards are incredibly consistent, and after years of using different models, I've never encountered more than the occasional bug. Lately, I've noticed that sometimes the keyboards are slow to wake from sleep mode, which can usually be fixed by toggling the power switch or connecting a cable.

Beyond that hiccup, I have zero issues.

My desk setup looks and feels great with a big mechanical keyboard at its center. The feet in the back let me raise the rear enough to ensure I'm at a comfortable typing angle too.

Uncompromised affordability

As I said at the top, I had to squint at the spec list to make sure I understood exactly why the K2 was half the price of the Q1. It comes down to build materials and switch options, but still.

At this price, the K2 Ultra 8K is a great option and hands-down a better option than Apple's Magic Keyboard. Sure, it's huge and heavy by comparison, but I'm not talking about it from a portability standpoint.

There's really not much else I can say that I haven't said in many previous Keychron reviews. These are some solid keyboards and I'll be the first to let you know if that ever changes.

If you want something a bit lighter and more affordable, I can easily recommend the Keychron K2 Ultra 8K.

Keychron K2 Ultra 8K review - Pros

  • Half the price and lighter than the premium Q1 model
  • South-facing RGB are bright and incredibly customizable
  • Hot-swappable switches, custom software, and a good typing experience
  • Connect up to 5 devices at once
  • Up to 760 hours of battery

Keychron K2 Ultra 8K review - Cons

  • No knob option
  • Lack of pre-configured color options
  • Would be nice if Keychron Launcher worked on iPad

Rating 4 out of 5

Since we have to give a numeric score, I can only say that Keychron continues to make almost perfect keyboards. They're expensive, and perhaps a little overkill for some, but they are great products.

Where to buy the Keychron K2 Ultra 8K

Get the Keychron K2 Ultra 8K mechanical keyboard from the Keychron website or Amazon for $119.99. It is only available fully assembled in black, though you get to choose between the Apex red, brown, or banana switch.
